plan.topic: Semaglutide and the GLP-1 class and age-related macular degeneration: the AAO 2026 case-control abstract, reused from the verified 10-22 Short
plan.angle: Minimum-effort carousel built only from the verified, published 10-22 Short script, with no new research. Slides: (1) the worry, named as understandable; (2) the crude 1.68 odds, labelled 'crude'; (3) what happened after adjusting for diabetes, blood pressure or cholesterol one at a time, and for age, each figure with its exact label as verified; (4) confounding explained in one line; (5) 'case-control · observational · conference abstract, not peer-reviewed (AAO, Oct 2026) · GLP-1 class · not shown to harm or protect'; (6) the EMA lists NAION as a very rare side effect of semaglutide (exact verified wording); keep regular eye exams, and get urgent care for any sudden vision change; (7) common GI side effects, 'don't stop or change your medicines on your own', 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line. No emoji.

package.title: Semaglutide, GLP-1s and Macular Degeneration: What One Study Can't Say

social.instagram_caption:
Worried semaglutide could hurt your eyes? That's a completely fair question to ask.

A new AAO 2026 conference abstract looked at GLP-1 medicines as a class and age-related macular degeneration in US health records.

The raw numbers showed a link. But adjusting for diabetes, blood pressure or high cholesterol (each one at a time) flipped the link the other way, which still doesn't mean protection. Adjusting for BMI weakened it. Adjusting for age strengthened it.

That's confounding at work: a link isn't a cause, and this one study can't settle it either way.

Separately, PRAC (the EMA's safety committee) said on 6 June 2025 that NAION, a different eye condition, is a very rare semaglutide side effect, affecting up to 1 in 10,000 people. Sudden vision changes need urgent care.

Save this for your next eye exam, and share it with a friend who has the same worry. Don't stop or change your medicines on your own.

#GLP1 #GLP1Medicines #Semaglutide #MacularDegeneration #EyeHealth #MetabolicHealth

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

slides.headline: Worried semaglutide could hurt your eyes?
slides.bubble: Totally fair worry. Let's read it together.

slides.headline: Crude odds ratio: GLP-1 use and AMD
slides.body: Unadjusted. US health records (Epic Cosmos): people with age-related macular degeneration compared with people without, GLP-1 class (AAO 2026 case-control abstract). An odds ratio, not an absolute risk.

slides.headline: Then researchers adjusted for other factors
slides.body: Each factor was adjusted for one at a time. Adjusting for diabetes, blood pressure or cholesterol flipped the link for any AMD (0.69, 0.65, 0.63). Adjusting for BMI weakened it; adjusting for age strengthened it. Mixed signals, not an answer.

items.label: Adjust for BMI
items.detail: Odds ratio fell to 1.17 (adjusted; AMD type not specified in report)

items.label: Adjust for age
items.detail: Odds ratio rose to 1.94 (adjusted; AMD type not specified in report)

slides.headline: A link proves the drug caused it
slides.body: Not here. GLP-1 users often have diabetes, high blood pressure or high cholesterol, which can travel with eye disease. That's confounding: another factor behind the link. Adjusting for those flipped the result, so this study can't show cause either way.

factcheck.summary: I checked every number, attribution and date against all three cited sources, and they match. S1 (HealthDay via Medical Xpress, 21 Oct 2026) describes a case-control analysis of Epic Cosmos records presented at the AAO meeting in New Orleans, 9–12 Oct 2026. Its figures match the slides: a crude odds ratio of 1.68 for any AMD, and odds ratios for any AMD of 0.69 after adjusting for type 2 diabetes, 0.65 for high blood pressure and 0.63 for high cholesterol, each factor adjusted one at a time. The report gives "attenuated to 1.17 with adjustment for body mass index" and "an increase in odds ratios to 1.94" for age without naming an AMD type, so the slide note "AMD type not specified in report" is accurate. S2 (PRAC meeting highlights, published 6 June 2025) says NAION is a very rare side effect of semaglutide that may affect up to 1 in 10,000 people, and that patients with sudden vision loss or rapidly worsening eyesight should "contact their doctor without delay". The slide says the same. S3 (the NHS semaglutide page) lists diabetic retinopathy getting worse as a serious side effect, and nausea, vomiting, constipation and diarrhoea among the common ones. The framing is sound: it says the result is observational and only shows a link, flags confounding, says the abstract covers the GLP-1 class rather than one drug, notes it's a conference abstract with no peer-reviewed paper yet, and says an odds ratio isn't an absolute risk. The "harm or protect" line doesn't claim more than the study shows. On safety, the slides tell people with sudden vision changes to get urgent care, tell them not to stop or change medicines on their own, and include "Not personal advice" and the prescriber line. They leave out PRAC's "stop treatment if confirmed" wording, which is right because it would read as stopping advice. The title and hook are fully paid off. I found no issues.
